doc.title: Alan Broadbent interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, October 26, 2023

title: Arranging for Paul McCartney's 'Kisses on the Bottom' and Natalie Cole
summary: Asked how he approaches a familiar tune, Broadbent describes his restrained charts for the McCartney album produced with Diana Krall, and his idea of a 'sub-song' under a standard.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Nice history. Arranging is hard to define sometimes but when you’re presented with a commission or a job or simply curiosity, to arrange something that is a common well known tune — I’m thinking — I wasn’t going to get to Paul McCartney right away but I was struck by the fact that you were involved in that record “Kisses On The Bottom” and you did the chart on “My Valentine,” one of his. But you also did one on “Bye Bye Blackbird.” So my question is, when you’re presented with this task of a well known tune, how do you conceive of a different and new setting for it?

Well, Monk, I don’t. I was invited by Diana Krall, who was involved in producing this album with Paul. And I’ve known Diana since she was like 19. She studied with me one summer when she came down from Canada. And so we’ve had a wonderful professional relationship in all that time. So she and Paul and her rhythm section had already put down the tracks. And Tommy LiPuma — a wonderful, wonderful guy — basically didn’t want me somehow to get in the way. And I know exactly when he meant is that what they need is not something which would be inappropriate, to suddenly soar over the strings and do the whole bit, you know whatever. It’s not appropriate to the task as you said. So it’s a craft and it’s a craft of knowing well yes, it could use a carpet here, you know? And if I could just do a simple line over the top there in this space, so I’ll be in this space and the chord space will be under here. It’s a very mathematical, you know, visual thing that you can do with orchestrating like this, people and their place. And then you just sort of sit back and stare at the blank page until, you know, when I see this movement I know what the chords are and perhaps I can get some counterpoint, a little subtle thing in there just so the sensitive listener can say, “Oh that’s Alan there, I just heard, for half a bar.”

An Alanism, yes. That takes a lot of — a certain attitude, some restraint, and as you said there’s a craft in that as well, to be satisfied that you’ve added a small bit that makes the whole that much better.

That’s the point. That’s the point. And there are other projects I have where the producer or the artist just, “Go!” You know. And I go — appropriately so you know. Because I’m always moving: composer, arranger, you know I’m moved by the situation. I’m not trying to outdo it or anything. I always want to be a part of this song, create some kind of sub- song underneath it as I like to put it, so that I have another song going on, even with say © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

Natalie Cole singing “Stardust” I have another “Stardust” going on, however subtley so I can add that way and to me it has a subliminal effect on people because we’re tuned to recognize things when we’re listening to them. So there’s a way of setting up those recognitions and orchestration, a little phrase or something. A person might not know because they’re only hearing this top line, but Alan under here is adding something, “Oh, what is that?” So that’s my goal is that in a standard song that I can pretend to be Mahler, whatever. No, not pretend, I can actually move people you know. And usually if I am moved at that point I know that yeah, okay, that means something. Whereas I never learned the craft (if you like) of well mediocrity. Mediocrity. I mean the craft of just knowing it all without any passion you know. And whatever I’m doing in music it has to be about some kind of passion because that’s what I do.
